title: SLO Alignment to Business Outcomes and Capacity Commitment Playbook
author: Liam Chen
content:
Overview
========

This playbook describes the CCSW (Capacity Commitments and SLO Weighting) framework: a practical, repeatable process to align SLOs and error budgets to measurable business outcomes, and to translate those commitments into concrete capacity provisioning, runbook actions, and incident evidence requirements. It is intended for SREs, product owners, and platform engineers responsible for Redwood inference services (hosted and dedicated).

Why this exists
---------------
- Reduce ambiguous SLO discussions by tying SLOs to customer-facing KPIs (throughput, latency, cost per token, and request-level correctness).
- Create capacity commitments that are auditable, provable, and reversible (so teams can safely trade error budget for capacity and vice versa).
- Standardize incident evidence and triage so postmortems map directly back to SLO weights and business impact.

Scope
-----
Applies to: inference-router, model-proxy, kv-cache, batching-service, capacity-orchestrator, and tenant-facing API gateways across hosted/dedicated/private deployments. Not in scope: offline tooling (training pipelines), billing pipeline internals.

Principles
----------
1) Map each SLO to a single business outcome (conversion, engagement, SLA credit liability).
2) Express SLOs as composite budgets when a user flow crosses multiple services (use SLO weight fractions).
3) Maintain a 72-hour proof window for capacity changes (shadow traffic + synthetic canaries) before full activation.
4) Keep emergency capacity steps reversible with automated rollback triggers.

Key concepts and definitions
----------------------------
- SLO: The measurable target (e.g., p99 latency < 350ms for text-generation requests).
- Error budget: 1 - SLO (e.g., 0.001 if SLO = 99.9%).
- SLO weight: Fraction of an end-to-end SLO allocated to a specific service. Sum(weights) = 1 for the flow.
- Capacity commitment: A defined pool of GPU/CPU/token-throughput reserved to meet an SLO over a contract window (daily/weekly).
- Proof window: The observation window after a capacity change where telemetry must validate improvement.

SLO -> Business outcome mapping (example)
---------------------------------------
This example maps a product metric to service SLOs. Replace values with your product team’s targets.

Table: Example mapping (ASCII)
Service           | SLO metric           | Target     | Business KPI mapped
------------------|----------------------|------------|----------------------
inference-router  | p95 latency (ms)     | <= 120 ms  | UI responsiveness -> engagement (drop rate)
model-proxy       | p99 latency (ms)     | <= 350 ms  | API success conversion (purchase complete)
kv-cache          | cache hit rate       | >= 85%     | billing cost per token
batching-service  | token/sec per GPU    | >= 80k TPS  | unit cost reduction

SLO Weighting example
---------------------
- End-to-end customer SLO: 99.9% success for 0-2048 token generation requests.
- Weights: inference-router 0.2, model-proxy 0.5, kv-cache 0.15, batching 0.15.
- Each service maintains its own error budget and a shared incident coordination policy: if any single service uses >50% of its error budget in a 7-day rolling window, an SLO review and capacity action is triggered.

Capacity proofing: calculation recipe
-----------------------------------
1) Determine baseline throughput and latency distribution from a 30-day window. Collect: RPS, p95/p99 latency, token distribution by request length, cold-start rate, KV cache hit rate.
2) Define desired headroom H (recommended: 25% for steady workloads, 40% for burst-prone tenants).
3) Calculate required GPU pool size:
   - Measured tokens/sec per GPU (Tgpu) = historical_token_throughput / active_gpu_count
   - Required GPUs = ceil( (peak_tokens_per_sec * (1 + H)) / Tgpu )
4) Validate with synthetic traffic: run 72-hour shadow test (90th/95th percentile traffic pattern) and assert: p95 latency remains within target, error budget burn rate < expected.

Example numbers
- Historical peak tokens/sec: 240k tps
- Observed Tgpu: 80k tps per A100-equivalent serving gpu
- Headroom H: 30% -> multiplier 1.3
- Required GPUs = ceil((240k * 1.3) / 80k) = ceil(3.9) = 4 GPUs (reserve 1 extra for preemptible churn)

Runbook: Fast-Path Capacity Boost (Emergency)
--------------------------------------------
Trigger: Any of the following
1) SLO burn rate > 2x planned daily burn and projected breach within 6 hours.
2) Sustained p99 latency > 2x target for 15 minutes with correlated increase in retry traffic.
3) Business escalation (Sales/CS reports major customer-facing degradation).

Immediate steps (SRE on-call)
1) Acknowledge and declare incident channel (Slack #sre-incident-<service>).
2) Run quick diagnostic (commands):
   - curl -s http://metrics.internal/query?service=inference-router
   - kubectl -n redwood get pods -l app=batching-service -o wide
   - rcli capacity describe --service model-proxy --format json | jq '.'
3) If capacity shortage suspected, execute temporary scale policy:
   - capacity-orchestrator scale --service <service> --delta +25% --duration 3h --note "fast-path boost"
4) Open a Capacity Evidence doc (see Evidence checklist below) and stream telemetry to the incident channel.
5) If boost stabilizes SLOs, schedule a 72-hour proof window and start root-cause hypothesis.
6) If boost does not help, follow standard incident escalation (pager to senior SRE, throttle non-critical tenants, activate degradation flows).

Rollback rules
- Auto-rollback after 3h if proofing is not initiated.
- Manual rollback only when: 72-hour synthetic proof passed OR incident resolved and capacity not needed.

Error budget policy and arbitration
----------------------------------
- Normal cadence: Teams own their service-level error budgets and must run an SLO review when monthly burn > 20% of budget.
- Arbitration: If two services claim the same headroom and budget, the Capacity Arbitration Board (CAB) decides using the CCSW calculator and business KPI impact score (see Appendix B). CAB membership: 2 SREs, 1 Product PM, 1 Infra Eng. Decision recorded in the capacity ledger.

Incident evidence checklist (minimum required)
---------------------------------------------
- Time window (UTC): start / end
- Affected tenants list (top 10 by RPS)
- SLO metric timeseries: p50/p95/p99, burn rate per minute
- Capacity state snapshot: per-region GPU count, queue depth, preemption events
- Recent deploys / config changes (last 24h) with Git SHAs and rollout IDs
- Error logs with sample trace IDs (anonymize PII)
- Synthetic canary results during incident (if any)
- Correlated external signals: upstream 3rd-party latency, network failures

Operational tooling & dashboards (required views)
-----------------------------------------------
1) Service Health dashboard (per service): p50/p95/p99, requests/sec, error budget remaining, capacity utilization, queued requests.
2) Tenant Impact view: top 50 tenants by error budget consumption, per-tenant headroom, throttling state.
3) Capacity Orchestrator panel: current pool sizes, preemption events, scheduled scale jobs, proof windows.
4) Incident Evidence collector: attach runbook steps, links to logs, and capacity snapshots.
5) Synthetic Canary dashboard: last 30 days of canary runs and pass/fail trends.

Dashboard queries (metric names)
- redwood.requests.count{service="$SERVICE"}
- redwood.latency.p99_ms{service="$SERVICE",quantile="0.99"}
- redwood.token_throughput.per_gpu{gpu_type="A100"}
- redwood.cache.hit_rate{service="kv-cache"}
- redwood.error_budget.burn_rate{service="$SERVICE"}

SLO review checklist (when burn > threshold)
1) Confirm telemetry integrity (no missing data feeds).
2) Run SLO-weighted impact analysis for the past 7 days.
3) Propose capacity options: (a) temporary boost with proof window, (b) long-term commit + autoscale config change, (c) targeted optimization (quantization, batching tuning).
4) Write a one-page decision memo and get CAB approval.
5) If approved, schedule changes in maintenance window and update capacity ledger.

Change and rollout safety gates
------------------------------
- Every capacity-increasing change must pass a canary in two regions before global activation.
- Autoscale updates require staging traffic shadowing for 48 hours and synthetic proof > 95% of expected flows.
- Rollback automation: if p99 increases by >30% vs canary baseline in 10 minutes, auto-roll back and open incident.

Appendix A: CCSW calculator pseudocode
-------------------------------------
Inputs: historical_peak_tokens_per_sec, tokens_per_gpu, headroom_fraction, slo_weights, critical_tenants
Output: recommended_gpu_counts, recommended_proof_window_hours

PSEUDOCODE:
1) for each tenant in critical_tenants: compute tenant_peak = tenant_pct * historical_peak_tokens
2) pool = ceil((historical_peak_tokens * (1 + headroom_fraction)) / tokens_per_gpu)
3) allocate per-service pools by slo_weights
4) proof_window_hours = max(72, 24 * ceil(headroom_fraction * 10))

Appendix B: Business KPI impact score
------------------------------------
Score is a weighted sum (0-100):
- Revenue exposure (40%)
- Active users affected (30%)
- Legal/SLA exposure (20%)
- Strategic customer flag (10%)

Example: Revenue exposure high (40) + active users medium (20) + SLA low (5) + strategic customer (10) => 75/100 -> prioritize capacity boost.

Governance and cadence
----------------------
- Monthly SLO review: every first Tuesday, CAB meets to review high-burn services.
- Quarterly capacity audit: confirm that reserved commitment matches usage and renegotiate headroom.
- Post-incident: evidence must be attached to the incident ticket and an action assigned within 7 days.

Ownership matrix (RACI style)
----------------------------
- SLO definition: Product (R), SRE (A), Engineering (C), CAB (I)
- Capacity sizing: SRE (R), Infra Eng (A), Product (C)
- Emergency scale: On-call SRE (R/A), CAB notified (I)
- Postmortem and action tracking: On-call SRE (R), All stakeholders (C)

Frequently asked questions
--------------------------
Q: How do we split weights for shared infra (e.g., KV cache used by many flows)?
A: Use a proportional weighting by observed token or request contribution to the end-to-end flow. If many flows are small, apply a minimum floor weight (0.05) to ensure shared infra has skin in the game.

Q: What if proofing fails and latency remains high after capacity boost?
A: Roll back the boost, open a deep-dive incident, apply tenant-level throttles, and prioritize optimizations (batching/quantization) with product sign-off for longer-term commits.

Q: Can teams buy additional capacity without CAB approval?
A: Temporary boosts (<=72 hours) can be executed by on-call SRE with post-facto CAB notification. Any longer-term committed capacity requires CAB approval and ledger entry.
